title: H-1B Tech Workers Live in Constant Career-Prep Mode as AI Layoffs Reshape US Job Market
excerpt: With over 114,000 tech jobs eliminated in 2026 and AI reshaping hiring priorities, Indian professionals on H-1B visas face a shrinking window to stay employed — and stay in the country.
body:
• More than 114,000 tech workers have been laid off across nearly 150 companies in 2026, with Indian H-1B holders disproportionately affected.
  • AI-driven restructuring is eliminating traditional software roles while creating demand for specialized machine learning and data science skills.
  • Laid-off H-1B workers face a 60-day grace period to find new sponsorship, switch visa categories, or leave the US — a deadline growing harder to meet.

For Indian software engineers on H-1B visas in the United States, the era of steady employment and predictable career ladders is over. A brutal combination of AI-driven restructuring and mass layoffs has pushed thousands of visa-dependent workers into a state of perpetual readiness — constantly updating résumés, practicing interview questions, and scanning job boards even while employed.

The numbers tell the story. According to Layoffs.fyi, more than 114,000 employees across nearly 150 technology companies have lost their jobs in 2026. Meta cut around 8,000 positions globally as it redirected resources toward artificial intelligence. Amazon, Oracle, LinkedIn, and Cisco have all trimmed headcount. The first three months of 2026 alone saw 52,050 tech layoffs — a 40% jump from the same period last year, according to executive coaching firm Challenger, Gray & Christmas.

The Visa Clock Starts Ticking

For American workers, a layoff means financial stress and a job search. For H-1B holders, it triggers an immigration countdown. Under USCIS rules, laid-off H-1B workers have a 60-day grace period from their last working day — not their final pay date — to find a new sponsoring employer, switch visa categories, or prepare to leave the country.

"Families are now dealing with mortgage payments, apartment leases, children in schools, and uncertain immigration timelines all at once, with only 60 days to resolve it."

— Rajiv Khanna, US-based immigration attorney

That 60-day window is proving brutal in a market where hiring has slowed sharply. Workers who previously used B-2 visitor status as a stopgap now face heavier scrutiny. Khanna told Outlook Business that his team is seeing a significant spike in Requests for Evidence and Notices of Intent to Deny on change-of-status applications — at a scale he described as beyond anything seen previously in his career.

AI Changes Who Gets Hired

The layoffs are not a cyclical dip. Companies are reorganizing work around AI tools and automated systems, a shift that has hit entry-to-mid-level IT roles where Indian H-1B workers have long held a strong presence.

"Companies are increasingly looking for specialized engineers with machine learning and data science skills," said Adarsh ML, a product engineer at Ather Energy who tracks global engineering hiring trends, in an interview with Computerworld. "Job opportunities for people with zero to three or four years of experience are not really there anymore."

Pareekh Jain, CEO of Pareekh Consulting, put it bluntly: "Companies are not looking for H-1B now. They are building a local workforce and preferring green card holders and citizens." Employers are more selective about hiring visa-dependent workers than they were two or three years ago, especially when permanent residents and US citizens are more available.

The shift extends beyond hiring preferences. AI coding tools like GitHub Copilot, Claude, and ChatGPT are compressing the amount of routine development work, meaning companies need fewer developers for similar tasks. Team structures are changing: roles once filled by interns and entry-level hires are being replaced by AI agents.

The Diaspora Calculation

For many Indian professionals, the math has changed. Indians represent the single largest group of H-1B holders, accounting for 283,772 of the 406,348 approved H-1B petitions in FY2025, according to USCIS and the Department of Homeland Security.

Swapnil Sagar, a former Microsoft engineer, returned to Bengaluru from Houston in late 2025 after a layoff ended a decade spent in the United States on the F-1-to-OPT-to-H-1B path. His story, reported by VisaVerge, captures a growing sentiment. Life in India, he said, felt "freer because life was no longer governed by visas."

A Blind poll cited in media reports suggested nearly half of Indian professionals in the US would consider returning to India if they lost their jobs. India's expanding technology base — with global capability centers, startup hiring, and remote roles in Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Pune, and Mumbai — is giving returning professionals a viable alternative.

Policy changes have added another layer of pressure. A Trump administration executive order proposed raising the H-1B application fee to $100,000, though a court of appeals has temporarily stayed the measure. Since September 2025, onshore movement from India to the US has been largely frozen.

What's Next

The immediate outlook remains grim for H-1B developers. Sanchit Vir Gogia, chief analyst at Greyhound Research, told Computerworld that developers must now build deeper expertise in cloud infrastructure, data engineering, security, and AI governance — skills closer to the systems enterprises need to validate and scale.

"The engineer who only produces output grows easier to replace as the output grows easier to generate. The engineer who can validate it, secure it, situate it in a real business, and stand behind the result becomes harder to replace."

— Sanchit Vir Gogia, chief analyst, Greyhound Research

For H-1B workers, adaptation now requires visa planning alongside career planning. "The strategic error is treating that window as a safety net rather than a planning horizon," Gogia added. As AI continues to reshape tech employment, the H-1B workforce — once the backbone of Silicon Valley's engineering talent — finds itself caught between an industry that wants fewer of them and an immigration system that gives them almost no room to adjust.
nri_angle: Indian nationals hold the majority of H-1B visas and are disproportionately affected by AI-driven tech layoffs, with many weighing a return to India as the US immigration system offers little flexibility.
author: Diaspora Desk
